title: The Chess Prodigy Who Hated Competition
book: Zero to One: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future
author: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters
wiifm: Yesterday Adam Smith showed how competition drives profit down to the ordinary rate. Today you follow a man who spent his youth winning competitions and concluded they are a trap. Peter Thiel was a chess prodigy, a top student and a law graduate on the fast track, and his career only took off when he stepped off it. The ideas he drew from that life, about monopoly, starting small, distribution and the power law, are directly useful to anyone running a brokerage or a lead generation business in a crowded market.

b: Peter Thiel was born in Frankfurt on the eleventh of October 1967, and his family moved to the United States when he was a baby. His father, Klaus, was a chemical engineer who worked on mining projects, and the work kept the family moving. Before Peter was ten he had lived in Cleveland, in South Africa, and in the desert town of Swakopmund in what is now Namibia, where his father worked on a uranium mine. He went to schools where pupils wore uniforms and were caned, and he later said he spent much of his time there exploring the desert alone.

In 1977 the family settled in Foster City, a suburb south of San Francisco, and Peter became the kind of child American schools are built to reward. He was a mathematics prodigy who won state competitions, and a chess player good enough to rank among the best in the country for his age. He kept a travel chess set, the story goes, with a sticker on it that read Born to Win.

He also became, in his own words later, a person whose life was a sequence of competitions. High school led to Stanford, where he studied philosophy and graduated in 1989. Stanford led to Stanford Law School, which he finished in 1992. Each stage was a contest with a clear winner, and he kept winning.

At Stanford he also founded a student newspaper, the Stanford Review, in 1987, as a contrarian voice on campus. Several of the people who wrote for it later turned up at PayPal. The habit of arguing against the consensus, which the book would make famous, was formed in a student magazine long before it was applied to money.
ch.cap: Young Peter plays chess alone in the Namibian desert

ch.h: The clerkship he did not get
b: After law school Thiel clerked for a federal appeals judge and then aimed for the top prize in American law: a clerkship at the Supreme Court. He reached the final interviews, with Justices Scalia and Kennedy, and was turned down. He describes being devastated. It was the first major contest he had lost.

He went to work instead at the elite New York law firm Sullivan and Cromwell. He lasted seven months and three days, a figure he quotes precisely. From the outside, he wrote, everyone wanted to get in, and from the inside, everyone wanted to get out. He moved on to trading derivatives at Credit Suisse, and then in 1996 went back to California to start a small investment fund with money from friends and family.

Years later, a friend from the clerkship days congratulated him and said that if he had got the Supreme Court job, he would never have built anything. Thiel tells this story to make a point that sits at the centre of the book. We are trained, from school onwards, to compete for scarce prizes that everyone else also wants. Winning feels like proof of value. But people who fight hard for the same thing as everyone else end up, at best, slightly ahead in a crowded field.
That is the personal version of the economic argument he would later make. Competition, he came to believe, is not a sign of value. It is a way of destroying it.
ch.cap: Turned down for the Supreme Court, Thiel walks away

b: In 1998 Thiel gave a guest lecture at Stanford. In the audience was Max Levchin, a young programmer who had emigrated from Ukraine and who was full of ideas about cryptography. They started a company together called Confinity. After false starts with security software for handheld computers, they built a way to send money by email. They called it PayPal.

The company did not try to serve the whole world at once. It found that its most enthusiastic users were the PowerSellers on eBay, the people who sold goods on the auction site as a living. Thiel later put their number at around twenty thousand. They needed a better way to take payment than waiting for posted cheques, they all knew each other, and they were concentrated in one place. PayPal set out to win almost all of them, and did.

In March 2000 Confinity merged with X.com, a rival online bank founded by Elon Musk, and the combined business took the PayPal name. The early years were a fight against fraud, against the banks and against eBay's own payment service. The company floated on the stock market in February 2002, and in October that year eBay bought it for one and a half billion dollars. Thiel's share made him rich.

The early PayPal team went on to found or fund YouTube, LinkedIn, Yelp, Tesla's early growth and much else, and the press called them the PayPal Mafia. That gave Thiel unusual standing to talk about how new companies actually begin. His central lesson from PayPal was simple and counterintuitive: start with a tiny market you can actually dominate.
ch.cap: Money flies by email to twenty thousand eBay PowerSellers

ch.h: Half a million dollars and the power law
b: In the summer of 2004 a Harvard student named Mark Zuckerberg came to California with a social network called TheFacebook. In August Thiel lent the company five hundred thousand dollars, convertible into a stake of a little over ten per cent. It was his first outside investment in the business. When he sold most of his shares around and after the 2012 flotation, that half million had become more than a billion dollars.

In 2005 he co-founded a venture capital firm, Founders Fund, and he also helped start the data analysis company Palantir. From all this he drew what he calls the biggest secret in venture capital: the best investment in a successful fund equals or outperforms the entire rest of the fund combined.

This is a power law. Returns are not spread evenly, like heights in a crowd. One outcome is enormous, a few are decent, and most are nothing. The consequence is uncomfortable. If one bet will outperform all the others combined, then spreading your effort thinly guarantees that you own too little of the one thing that works.

Thiel applies this to lives as well as portfolios. He attacks what he calls indefinite optimism, the belief that the future will be better without any particular plan for how, which leads people to keep options open, build broad but shallow skills and prefer money to commitments. His alternative is definite optimism: a specific picture of a better future, and the work of building it. You are not a lottery ticket, he says.

There is an honest counterweight, and it comes from his own record. From 2002 he also ran a large macro hedge fund called Clarium Capital, which bet on big economic trends. It grew to more than seven billion dollars around 2008, then was battered by wrong calls on the markets and had shrunk to a few hundred million by 2011. The man arguing for strong definite views lost most of a fund to a definite view that was mistaken. That, too, is what a power law looks like from the inside.
ch.cap: A $500,000 cheque, and the power law behind it

b: In the spring of 2012 Thiel taught a course at Stanford called Computer Science 183: Startup. A law student named Blake Masters sat in the lectures typing detailed notes and posted them online after each class. Within weeks they were being passed round Silicon Valley and far beyond. Masters and Thiel turned the notes into a book, published in September 2014 with Masters credited as co-author. It sold in the millions.

That origin explains the book's tone. It is not a manual. It is a single sharp mind arguing with received opinion, aloud, in front of students. It opens with the question Thiel says he asks in job interviews: what important truth do very few people agree with you on?

He points out that this is hard for two reasons. Most people cannot think of an answer, which is a failure of thinking. And those who can are often unwilling to say it, which is a failure of nerve. Thiel thinks courage is even scarcer than brilliance.

The title gives the main framework. Going from one to n means copying what already works: more typewriters, or a proven business model rolled out in a new country. Thiel calls this globalisation. Going from zero to one means doing something new for the first time. He calls this technology, in the broad sense of any new way of doing more with less. Copies are safer, but their profits are competed away. Genuinely new things are risky, and when they work they are the only things that really pay.
ch.cap: Blake Masters types notes as Thiel teaches CS183

b: The heart of the book is a deliberate twist on the opening line of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina. All happy companies are different, Thiel writes: each one earns a monopoly by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the same: they failed to escape competition.

This is Adam Smith read backwards. Under perfect competition, firms sell interchangeable products, nobody has power over price, and profit is driven down to cost. Economists call this efficient. Thiel points out that it describes a business you should not want to own.

His example uses figures from 2012. American airlines took about a hundred and sixty billion dollars in revenue, carrying a vast number of passengers at an average one-way fare of about a hundred and seventy-eight dollars. Yet by his calculation they made about thirty-seven cents of profit per passenger trip. Google took around fifty billion dollars in revenue, kept about twenty-one per cent as profit, and was worth roughly three times as much as every American airline combined. The airlines create enormous value. They capture almost none of it, because they compete it away in cheap fares. Creating value and capturing value, Thiel insists, are different things.

He then explains why you cannot simply ask a company which kind it is. Monopolies pretend to be small: Google describes itself as one technology company among many, competing in advertising, phones and everything else, so its share of any market looks modest. Competitive businesses pretend to be special: the restaurant that calls itself the only Nepalese and Japanese fusion place in the area. One defines its market as huge to hide its power. The other defines its market as tiny to invent some. Both are distorting the picture, in opposite directions.
ch.cap: A full airliner earns thirty-seven cents a passenger

b: Thiel lists four features of a business that can hold on to its profits, and the value of the list is that it is short. If your advantage is not one of these, he suggests, it is probably not an advantage.

First, proprietary technology, and his rule of thumb is that it must be about ten times better than the nearest substitute on something that matters. Thirty per cent better feels to customers like a small improvement and is treated as one. Second, network effects, where a product becomes more useful as more people use it. Such businesses must start very small, because the product must be valuable to its first users before the network exists. Facebook began at one university, where everyone you knew really was on it. Third, economies of scale, where the cost of serving each extra customer falls as you grow. Software has this; a yoga studio, which needs another hour of someone's time for every new client, does not. Fourth, branding, which Thiel calls real but dangerous, because it cannot be built on nothing.

From this comes his strategy: start small, dominate, then expand. Dominating a small market is possible; winning one per cent of a giant market gives you no foothold. PayPal began with the eBay sellers, Amazon with books, Facebook with Harvard. Each widened outwards into neighbouring markets.

And he demolishes a favourite business cliché. First-mover advantage, he argues, is a tactic mistaken for a goal. What matters is to be the last mover, to make the last great development in a market and enjoy years of monopoly profits. Google was not the first search engine, nor Facebook the first social network. Each was the last one that mattered.
ch.cap: Facebook's network spreads from one campus's dorm windows

b: Thiel's sharpest practical chapter is about distribution, the part engineers and owner-operators both tend to neglect. If you have invented something new but have not invented an effective way to sell it, he writes, you have a bad business, however good the product.

The test is the relationship between what a customer is worth to you over their whole relationship and what it costs to win them. He describes a ladder of methods. At the top are complex sales: very large deals, closed personally by the founder, a handful a year. Below that is personal selling by a sales team. Then marketing and advertising, and at the bottom viral growth, where customers bring other customers almost for free. The method must match the value. You cannot send a salesperson to sell something worth a few hundred pounds, and you cannot sell a million pound system through adverts.
Between them lies what he calls a dead zone: products too expensive to sell through advertising alone, too cheap to pay for a salesperson. Companies stall there for years without understanding why.

He closes with seven questions every business must answer. Engineering: is your product a breakthrough or a small improvement? Timing: is this the right moment? Monopoly: are you starting with a big share of a small market? People: do you have the right team? Distribution: can you reach customers, not just make something? Durability: will your position hold in ten or twenty years? And the secret: have you seen an opportunity others have not? Companies that answer five or six well, he claims, tend to succeed. Durability and distribution are where established small firms most often fail.
ch.cap: The distribution ladder, with a dead zone in the middle

b: The book rewards a sceptical reader, so here are its weak points. Its claim that monopoly is good is a statement about what is good for companies, dressed up as one about society. Thiel argues that monopoly profits fund innovation, which is sometimes true and is also exactly what every monopolist has always said. Customers of a monopoly pay more today, and the promised benefits arrive later, if at all.

It also suffers badly from survivorship bias. Its evidence is a handful of giant winners studied after the fact. There is no count of the many firms that started small, pursued a secret and monopolised nothing.

Some predictions have aged poorly. Thiel used the clean technology crash of the 2000s to argue that the sector failed his tests. Since then, the price of lithium-ion batteries and solar panels has fallen dramatically, with industry surveys putting battery pack prices at around a hundred dollars per kilowatt-hour by 2025, a small fraction of the level when he wrote. The firms he criticised were often bad businesses. The technology was not a dead end.

And his favourite monopolies have since met the courts. In August 2024 a federal judge ruled that Google held an illegal monopoly in search, though the remedies imposed in 2025 stopped short of breaking it up. In November 2025 another federal judge ruled that the Federal Trade Commission had failed to prove that Meta, Facebook's parent company, held monopoly power. Durable monopoly can survive the law, but how you got it matters.

None of this cancels the core insight, which is simply correct. Competition competes away profit. If you want to keep some of the value you create, you need something rivals genuinely cannot copy. Tomorrow you will meet a man who built the most complete monopoly in industrial history, not with a new technology, but with barrels, ledgers and a railway contract.
ch.cap: A federal judge rules Google holds an illegal monopoly

take: Profit lives where rivals cannot easily follow. Ask what about your business a competitor genuinely could not copy within a year, and invest in that before anything else.
Write your market as your marketing describes it, then as a hostile analyst would. Your real position is the second one, and the gap tells you which advantages are load-bearing.
PayPal won a small, connected group before the world. Identify the narrow customer segment you could realistically dominate, and win it completely before widening.
Ten times, not ten per cent
A small improvement is treated as a small improvement. Look for the one dimension where your offer could be dramatically better than the alternative, and focus there.
Match the channel to the value
Compare what a customer is worth over their lifetime with what it costs to win them. If the ratio is thin, change the channel or raise lifetime value rather than pushing harder in the same place.
A few clients, channels or products usually produce most of the results. Find your biggest one and give it a disproportionate share of your time and money.
Aim to be the last mover
Being first matters little if you are gone in five years. Ask why, when your market settles, it should settle on you.
Keep both halves of the story
Thiel's Facebook bet and his Clarium losses came from the same confident mind. Treat any successful person's advice as a hypothesis, not a rule.
recall: What is the difference between going from zero to one and from one to n?

One to n is copying and scaling what already works, which Thiel calls globalisation. Zero to one is creating something new for the first time, which he calls technology. Copies are safer but their profits get competed away.
What are the four features of a business that keeps its profits?
Proprietary technology, ideally about ten times better than the nearest substitute; network effects; economies of scale; and branding built on real substance.
Why did PayPal start with eBay PowerSellers?

Because a small, concentrated market of around twenty thousand people could be dominated quickly, and they badly needed the product. From a dominated small market a company can expand outward; from one per cent of a huge market it cannot.
What is the power law in venture capital, and what is its practical lesson?
The best investment in a successful fund equals or beats all the others combined. So spreading effort evenly means owning too little of the one thing that works; concentration is rewarded.
What is the distribution dead zone?

The price range where a product is too expensive to sell through advertising alone but too cheap to justify a salesperson. Firms stuck there have no viable way to win customers and often never realise why growth stalls.
note: Biographical details come from Thiel's own accounts in the book and interviews, and from Max Chafkin's 2021 biography The Contrarian; the Born to Win chess set is his own anecdote. Airline and Google figures are Thiel's 2012 calculations as given in the book. Clarium's peak and decline are widely reported estimates. Critiques reflect contemporary reviews; the 2024 Google ruling and 2025 Meta ruling are matters of public record.
words: Holding opinions that go against the accepted or official view.
Thiel's interview question, what important truth do very few people agree with you on, is a demand for a heterodox belief and the nerve to say it.
Owned exclusively by one person or company and protected from copying.
Thiel's first test of a lasting advantage is proprietary technology about ten times better than the nearest substitute.
Describing a loan or bond that can be swapped for shares in the company instead of being repaid.
In 2004 Thiel lent Facebook five hundred thousand dollars as a convertible loan, which turned into a stake of a little over ten per cent.
A pattern in which a tiny number of outcomes are enormous and most are small, rather than results clustering around an average.
Thiel calls the power law the biggest secret in venture capital: the best investment in a good fund outperforms all the rest combined.
The error of drawing lessons only from the winners who survived, while ignoring the many who tried the same thing and vanished.
Critics note that Zero to One studies a handful of giant successes and never counts the startups that followed the same rules and failed.
stories: Peter Thiel was a chess prodigy, a maths champion, a Stanford graduate and a Stanford law graduate. He had won every contest he entered. Then he reached the final interviews for a Supreme Court clerkship, the top prize in American law, with Justices Scalia and Kennedy, and was turned down. Devastated, he joined an elite New York law firm instead and lasted seven months and three days, a figure he still quotes exactly. Years later an old friend congratulated him: if you had got that clerkship, you would never have built anything. Losing the race everyone wanted to win was the best thing that ever happened to him.

When PayPal began, it could have tried to sell online payments to the whole world. Instead it found its keenest users were eBay PowerSellers, people who sold goods on the auction site for a living. Thiel put their number at around twenty thousand. They all needed a faster way to get paid than waiting for posted cheques, they all knew each other, and they were all in one place. PayPal set out to win nearly every one of them, and did. From that tiny beachhead it spread outwards, and in 2002 eBay itself bought PayPal for one and a half billion dollars. Dominate something small first.

In 2012, Thiel calculated, American airlines took about a hundred and sixty billion dollars in revenue, carrying passengers at an average one way fare of around a hundred and seventy-eight dollars. Their profit per passenger trip came to roughly thirty-seven cents. In the same year Google took about fifty billion dollars and kept around a fifth of it as profit. The punchline: Google was worth roughly three times every American airline combined. Airlines create enormous value, getting millions of people across a continent, and capture almost none of it, because they compete it away. Creating value and keeping it are different skills.
biz: PayPal won one small connected group before the world. For HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan, pick one segment you could genuinely serve better than anyone, for example self-employed homeowners borrowing for home improvements, where lender knowledge really helps. This week, pull six months of enquiries and compare conversion rate and cost per completed loan by segment. Then build one SEO page, one ad group and one call script for that segment only, and track whether you become the obvious choice there. Choose the segment for where you add real value, never for where customers are easiest to rush.
Measure cost per completed loan, not per lead

Thiel's distribution test compares what a customer is worth with what it costs to win them. Cost per lead flatters some channels. For each of Google, Bing, Facebook and organic, calculate spend divided by completed loans, set against the average commission earned. A channel with cheap leads that rarely complete may sit in his dead zone. Share the figures with whoever runs the ad accounts and agree changes from evidence. Watch the other side too: if a channel only works when callers are pushed harder, that is a Consumer Duty problem, not a sales opportunity.
connects: Thiel reads Smith's machine, in which competition drives profit down to the ordinary rate, and argues that the protected exceptions are the only part worth owning.
Thiel's power law, where one investment outweighs all the others, is the same world of extreme, lopsided outcomes that Taleb calls Extremistan.
Thiel's advice to dominate a small market before expanding mirrors the positioning idea of owning one narrow slot in the customer's mind before reaching wider.
recap:
Peter Thiel was built to win. Born in Frankfurt in nineteen sixty-seven, he spent part of his childhood in a desert town in Namibia, where his father worked on a uranium mine, and then grew up in California as a maths prodigy and one of the best young chess players in the country. Stanford, then Stanford Law School. Every stage was a contest, and he kept winning.

Then he lost. He reached the final interviews for a Supreme Court clerkship and was turned down. He joined a grand New York law firm and lasted seven months and three days. Years later a friend told him that if he had got that clerkship he would never have built anything. That became the root of his philosophy: fighting hard for the prize everyone else wants is a trap.

In nineteen ninety-eight he co-founded the company that became PayPal. It did not try to serve the world. It set out to win about twenty thousand eBay PowerSellers, people who all knew each other and badly needed a better way to get paid. Having won them, it spread, and eBay bought it for one and a half billion dollars. Thiel then lent Facebook half a million dollars, which became more than a billion.

From a Stanford class in twenty twelve, written up from a student's notes, came Zero to One. Its first big idea is that competition destroys profit. American airlines carried vast numbers of people and made about thirty-seven cents on each trip, while Google was worth around three times all of them combined. Creating value and capturing value are different things.

The second idea is that lasting advantage comes from a short list: technology about ten times better than the alternative, network effects, economies of scale, and a brand built on something real.

The third is to start small, dominate, then widen, and to aim to be the last mover in a market rather than the first.

The fourth is that distribution matters as much as the product. Match the way you sell to what a customer is worth, and beware the dead zone where neither adverts nor salespeople pay for themselves.

The fifth is the power law. One bet often outperforms all the others combined, so spreading yourself thin means owning too little of what works. Yet Thiel's own hedge fund shrank badly after confident calls went wrong, the book leans heavily on survivors, and the courts have since examined his favourite monopolies.

His opening question is the line to keep. What important truth do very few people agree with you on?
